title: Cut Text Into Sealed Pieces
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Cut it into consecutive pieces so that each letter appears in at most one piece: every copy of a letter lives in the same piece. Make as many pieces as possible.

Return the lengths of the pieces, from left to right. Joined in order, the pieces give back s.

examples.why: "aba" holds every a and b, and "cdcd" holds every c and d. No smaller cut keeps the a's or the c's together.
Cutting right after the last x (at index 2) would split the two y's. The first piece has to stretch to the last y, which pulls in the z too.
No letter repeats, so every letter can be its own piece. The answer wants the most pieces, not just any valid cut.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
hints: Look at the first letter. Its piece has to reach at least as far as which index?
Every letter you pass on the way also drags the end of the piece out to its own last copy. When can you finally cut?
Record each letter's last index. Walk left to right, keeping end = the largest last index seen in the current piece. When your position equals end, cut there.

explain.intuition:
The first piece must contain the last copy of s[0]. And every letter inside the piece pulls the end out to its own last copy. So walk from the left, keeping end = the furthest last copy of any letter seen so far in this piece. When your index reaches end, every letter in the piece has all its copies inside: the piece is sealed.

Why cutting at the first sealed point never hurts: no valid cut can come earlier, because some letter would be split. And cutting there costs nothing later, because the rest of the string uses none of the letters before the cut, so it can be cut exactly as if it were a fresh string. Taking the earliest possible cut every time therefore gives the most pieces. It is the same picture as merging intervals: each letter is the interval from its first to its last copy, and pieces are the merged groups.
steps: First pass: record last[c], the last index of each letter.
Second pass: keep start and end of the current piece. At index i, set end = max(end, last[s[i]]).
If i == end, the piece is sealed: push end − start + 1 and set start = i + 1.
pitfalls: Ending the piece at the last copy of its first letter only. Example 2 shows a later letter can push the end further.
Returning start or end indices instead of lengths, or forgetting the + 1 in end − start + 1.
Calling lastIndexOf inside the loop. It is correct but turns the scan into O(n²) on long strings.

solutions.title: Grow each piece with lastIndexOf
solutions.idea: Same walk, but look up each letter's last copy by searching the string every time.

solutions.title: Last-index table, cut when sealed
solutions.idea: Precompute each letter's last index. Stretch the current piece to the furthest last index seen; cut as soon as you reach it.

followups: Return the pieces themselves as strings. What does that change in memory use?
Now you want the fewest pieces of length at most L, with the same sealing rule. Does a greedy still work?
